desc:
You are given a string s and a dictionary, written as one string words where the dictionary words are separated by commas, for example "abc,xyz,ab". A word can be made from s by deleting some (possibly zero) characters of s without reordering the rest, that is, if the word is a subsequence of s.

Return the longest dictionary word that can be made from s. If several have the longest length, return the one that is smallest in dictionary (alphabetical) order. If no word can be made, return "-".

For example, s = "xaybzc" with words = "abc,xyz,ayz,xbc,ab,az" gives "abc": four words of length 3 can be made, and abc is the alphabetically smallest. With s = "abc" and words = "d,e" the answer is "-".
constraints: The dictionary has between 1 and 1,000 words; each word has 1 to 50 lowercase letters (duplicates may occur)
s consists of lowercase letters; words contains lowercase letters and commas only, with no empty word
hints: For each word you only need a yes/no answer: is it a subsequence of s?
Use one pointer on s and one on the word. Move through s; every time the characters are equal, advance the pointer in the word. The word fits when its pointer reaches the end.
Keep the best word so far and replace it when the new word is longer, or equally long and alphabetically smaller. No sorting is needed.
editorial: Split words at commas. For each word run the standard two-pointer subsequence test: scan s once, and each time s[i] equals the next needed letter of the word, move to the next needed letter. If all letters were matched in order, the word can be made.

Among feasible words keep the one with larger length, breaking ties by the smaller string. Each test costs O(|s|) in the worst case (or less when using a jump such as find from the last matched position), so the total is O(|s| · W) for W words. A pre-sorted dictionary (by length descending, then alphabetically) lets you stop at the first feasible word, but the single pass is simpler and as fast in the worst case.
